entries.title: Water conflict around the German capital
entries.summary: Though the German state of Brandenburg that wraps around Berlin is getting drier, it is also home to thirsty industrial plants such as Tesla, Red Bull. Is there enough water to go around?
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Though the German state of Brandenburg that wraps around Berlin is getting drier, it is also home to thirsty industrial plants such as Tesla, Red Bull. Is there enough water to go around?

For years, Petra Liesenfeld has witnessed falling groundwater levels in her hometown of Baruth. She has to water her garden far more often than she used to, and has seen some local trees completely dry out. At the same time, two beverage companies are looking to expand production in the area.

Mineral water has been bottled in the small town of Baruth, which lies around 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin, since the 1990s. The site is now run by Red Bull and Austrian beverage producer Rauch, who are planning a new canning factory and additional facilities. All in the middle of a water protection area.

The Baruth waterworks are licensed to extract a fixed amount of groundwater each year, just 8% of which goes to supply the town's roughly 4,300 residents with drinking water. The remaining 92% is reserved for Red Bull and Rauch, and is enough to cover the drinking water needs of 57,000 people. But exactly how much water the companies currently use is not made public.

This is legal under the existing contracts, said Peter Ilk, who until recently was the town's mayor and is considered a driving force behind the region's industrialization. He sees no problem with the way water is managed.

"We have always given priority to supplying the population. That is also written into all the contracts," he said, adding that it stands to reason that the companies need more than the town's residents. "That's how you end up with this ratio of around one to 10 in terms of consumption."

Old data informing current decisions

Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt from the Technical University in Berlin takes a more critical view, pointing out that the contracts, which are around 30 years old, are based on outdated information. Since then, groundwater levels, groundwater recharge and the way land is used have all changed significantly.

"I am concerned at how the water situation is developing in the state of Brandenburg," she said. "The volume that is actually available is currently being overestimated by the Brandenburg authorities."

Together with a citizens' initiative made up of local residents, she is calling for new, independent assessments — and for clear and open communication. Though the authorities granted them access to some groundwater monitoring documents, large parts were redacted, which some residents believe is a move to conceal information about changes in levels.

"We ask ourselves why there can't be more transparency if everything is aboveboard. Why isn't the public allowed to know?" said Petra Liesenfeld.

Exactly how much Red Bull and Rauch pay for their daily extraction of up to 7 million liters of groundwater is not public information.



DW approached both companies for comment, but by the time of publication, neither had responded.



For drought researcher Andreas Marx, this lack of transparency is problematic.

"By law, water is a public commodity. It cannot be privately owned. So, in my view, every decision made and every contract signed over its use should be open to the public," he said.

How dry is Brandenburg?

Germany — and Brandenburg — are still water-rich regions. Marx, who heads the Drought Monitor at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said "the challenge isn't adapting to permanent water scarcity but learning how to cope with dry periods that can last two or even three years."

Nevertheless, the water balance in the state, as elsewhere in Germany, is definitely changing. Since the 2018 drought, groundwater has not been sufficiently replenished in many places and higher temperatures and increasing evaporation are making it harder for reserves in deeper soil layers to recover.

This could cause even more problems in the future, as 95% of Brandenburg's drinking water comes from groundwater.

How much water does the energy transition need?

In Grünheide, in the eastern part of the state of Brandenburg, Tesla's Gigafactory has a permit to extract up to 1.4 million cubic meters of water per year and is planning to expand production to as many as 7,500 vehicles per week. Meanwhile, in recent years, residents have repeatedly been urged to save water.

"Many projects, including new schools and kindergartens, were put on hold because there simply wasn't enough water," said local resident Manu Hoyer.

Marx said when water resources are scarce, residents are generally the first to face restrictions because they're the easiest to limit. "Industrial companies are rarely restricted, because the economic consequences are much harder to assess," he said.

Copper for the energy transition — a risk to groundwater?

The potential for an additional water problem is brewing further south in Spremberg, where a large mine is planned. Over the coming decades, copper — which is essential for power grids, electric vehicles and the transition to clean energy — is set to be extracted from depths of up to 1,200 meters (about 4,000 feet).

Geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeiffer said mine water from such depths is highly saline and sulfurous and requires extensive treatment.

"But the treatment plant proposed so far is nowhere near capable of doing what's actually required to clean the water to a standard where it could be safely discharged into the Spree," Pfeiffer said of the river that flows north toward Berlin.



The river water is already affected by decades of lignite mining in the region, and it is facing additional pressures. With lignite extraction set to end by 2038, the groundwater currently pumped into the Spree from the mines will no longer be available. As a result, dry summers could see the river carrying up to 75% less water, with far-reaching consequences for water resources all the way to Berlin.

Could rainfall be stored for future use?

One possible solution to the water problems facing the state around the German capital is artificial groundwater recharge, where excess water from periods of high rainfall is stored underground and used later.

Hydrogeologist Engelhardt is researching where this could be possible in the region.

"There are areas in Brandenburg — such as where Tesla is now located — where artificial groundwater recharge could meet almost the entire demand of the local drinking water supplier," she said.

However, enough available water is necessary for this solution to work.

For drought researcher Marx, one question remains crucial: What rules should determine how water is distributed between the population, agriculture, nature and industry during prolonged dry periods?

As the global temperature continues to rise, it's not just an issue reserved for Brandenburg — or even Germany.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Israeli military to open criminal probes into 2 Gaza attacks
entries.summary: The investigations will focus on the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind ⁠Rajab and 15 emergency aid workers in Gaza. The decision came after a review of 150 incidents concerning the conduct of Israeli troops.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Israeli military to open criminal probes into 2 Gaza attacks

August 19, 2026

The investigations will focus on the killings of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind ⁠Rajab and 15 emergency aid workers in Gaza. The decision came after a review of 150 incidents concerning the conduct of Israeli troops.

The Israeli military has announced it will open criminal investigations into two high-profile attacks on Palestinians during the Gaza war.

In a report published Wednesday, the Israeli military said it had reviewed 150 incidents involving its troops in the Palestinian enclave and had made decisions about five of the cases.

The killings of 5-year-old Hind Rajab in 2024 and 15 Palestinian paramedics in 2025 would be subject to a criminal probe, the military said.

However, it said it would not take that step in the case of three other attacks in which aid workers from the charities World Central Kitchen and Doctors Without Borders were killed.

The killing of Hind Rajab and 8 others in Gaza City

On January 29, 2024, Israeli forces fired on a car approaching them that was carrying a 5-year-old Palestinian girl, Hind Rajab, and her relatives in Gaza City, the military said in its report.

Five of the passengers were killed, while Rajab and her 15-year-old cousin Layan Hamada survived. Layan called the Palestinian Red Crescent, telling them a tank was approaching and her family members had been killed. According to a Red Crescent recording of the call, gunshots were heard, and Layan went silent. Rajab then stayed on the phone with the Red Crescent for hours, trapped in the car, as they tried to get permission from the military to rescue her, but contact was lost.

An ambulance dispatched to the site was also allegedly hit by a shell as it arrived.

Twelve days later, the bodies of Hind and seven of her relatives were recovered from the scene, along with two paramedics. The case drew international outrage.

“Following review of the findings and due to alleged failures in the coordination of the movement of the Palestine Red Crescent ambulance, it has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident,” the Israeli military said in its report.

This article will be updated as reactions come in.

entries.title: Pakistan: Could ex-PM Imran Khan make a new deal?
entries.summary: The imprisoned former prime minister of Pakistan was moved to a hospital for medical treatment, ushering speculation over the possibility of new political negotiations.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan: Could ex-PM Imran Khan make a new deal?

August 19, 2026

The imprisoned former prime minister of Pakistan was moved to a hospital for medical treatment, ushering speculation over the possibility of new political negotiations.

Pakistan's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan to be shifted to a private hospital after Khan's family and political supporters repeatedly raised concerns about the 73 year old's deteriorating health in Rawalpindi's Adiala jail. 

The founder of the opposition party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has been imprisoned since August 2023 and is currently serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges he says are politically motivated.

The former prime minister was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Khan and his supporters say Pakistan's influential military is trying to keep him out of politics, an allegation the military denies.

Despite his remaining behind bars, Khan remains politically popular. Despite a crackdown on the PTI following Khan's arrest, the candidates backed by him performed strongly in the February 2024 elections.

"Three years in prison have not removed Khan from Pakistani politics. He remains PTI's biggest political asset, but the party's reliance on him has also exposed weaknesses in its leadership and organization," Raza Rumi, a US-based Pakistani political analyst, told DW.

Dousing speculation of a new deal for Khan

The transfer of Khan to the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical assessment has added a new dimension to the debate over his future and the possibility of political negotiations.

However, Khan's adviser Sayed Zulfi Bukhari rejected speculation that court decision was the result of any political deal with the government.

"There is no deal between Imran Khan and anyone. This is the Supreme Court's decision, which is very much welcomed," Bukhari said.

Pakistan's Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said in a video statement issued on Tuesday night that the government would challenge the Supreme Court order, claiming it was unlawful.

The minister said a convicted prisoner must be treated inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law, adding that he was requesting Khan's medical tests be carried out at a government hospital instead of a private facility.

"Legally, Khan has not been granted bail nor have his convictions been suspended. He will remain a prisoner, and the hospital executive ward shall serve as a sub-jail. Unfortunately, most ordinary prisoners with far more serious ailments are never allowed such facilities by the courts," Osama Malik, a legal expert, told DW.

Pakistan's Minister of State for Interior, Talal Chaudhry, told DW that "Khan's cases will be decided by the courts."

Khan's health problems

PTI's Bukhari told DW that Khan "hasn't been receiving the right medical care in prison."

"That is why it has got to this stage. He has been kept in complete solitude, which has deteriorated his health."

Khan's PTI party has said he's suffering from various health conditions, including poor eyesight, fluctuations in blood pressure, and anxiety linked to restricted contact with his family, and has been unable to access specialist medical care.

Some analysts think that the health concerns are now serious enough to have prompted Supreme Court intervention.

"Beyond the medical issues, this is also about trust. The PTI and Khan's family have repeatedly questioned his access to doctors and the transparency of his treatment," said analyst Rumi.

"After three years in prison, and given his age, any deterioration in his health carries major political consequences. The state, therefore, has every reason to ensure credible and transparent medical care," he added.

The court also ordered a medical board, including Khan's sister, Dr. Uzma Khan, and personal physician Dr. Faisal Sultan, to oversee his treatment.

The future of Khan and his PTI party

Khan's continued imprisonment has tested the PTI's ability to maintain its political strength, and the party's future will depend on whether it can maintain support without the direct political presence of its figurehead.

"Khan's political future does not look bright; he will have to compromise his political future. He will remain in jail, and even if his PTI party comes to power in the future, Khan will not be part of the government," Qamar Cheema, a political analyst, told DW.

At the same time, Khan's continued popularity makes it difficult for authorities to remove him completely from the political equation in Pakistan.

"For the state, the dilemma remains: keeping Khan imprisoned has not neutralized his influence, while releasing him without a broader settlement could revive the confrontation," remarked analyst Rumi.

Rumi added that any lasting political settlement with Khan would likely require an understanding with the military establishment, which remains a key stakeholder in Pakistan.

"Such a deal could involve legal relief for Khan, greater political space for PTI, and eventually his release, in return for PTI easing its confrontation with the military and pursuing a negotiated political process. But deep mistrust remains a major obstacle, while Khan's reluctance to compromise limits the prospects for a settlement," he said.

Analyst Cheema said he doesn't think there is any possibility of a deal between the government and Khan.

"This was a genuine understanding in the Supreme Court that he should have been given proper health care," he said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Amanal Petros: From refugee to European champion
entries.summary: Amanal Petros fled to Germany as a teenager. Now one of the world's top marathon runners, he recently won gold at the European Athletics Championships.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Amanal Petros fled to Germany as a teenager. Now one of the world's top marathon runners, he recently won gold at the European Athletics Championships.

Amanal Petros stood in Birmingham's Victoria Square, the German flag draped over his shoulders and the gold medal resting on his chest. Eleven months after narrowly missing out on a World Championship title in Tokyo, the 31-year-old had just won his first major marathon.

After roughly 25 of the 42 kilometers, Petros picked up the pace on an incline, breaking up the lead pack. No one could keep up with him. He was able to savor the victory during the final two kilometers. He crossed the finish line in 2:09:11 — a record time for the men's marathon at the European Athletics Championships.

"My goal was to wrap things up early," Petros said afterwards. "That worked out perfectly."

The fact that Italian runner Pietro Riva finished just seven seconds behind him hardly reflected the commanding nature of the victory. "I had everything under control," Petros added.

Late arrival

Issues entering the United Kingdom meant Petros didn't arrive in Birmingham until Saturday — the day before the race. Media reports indicated there were difficulties with his electronic travel authorization.

"It took a very, very long time; it was awful. We were traveling back and forth for two days," he recounted. The German Athletics Association (DLV) helped resolve the issues.

The following day, a course featuring eight laps, inclines, and numerous turns awaited the runners. Petros had spent months preparing for the event at altitude in Kenya.

"120 turns, the climbs. It was a huge challenge," he said.

Then Petros dedicated his gold medal to his mother.

"She is my queen and my source of strength," he stressed. "Thinking of her gives me new energy and motivation. She is simply the best."

His mother lives more than 5,000 kilometers (3,107 miles) away in the Tigray region of Ethiopia.

Coming to Germany alone at 16

Petros was born in the Eritrean port city of Assab in 1995. As a young child, he fled with his family — escaping the war between Eritrea and Ethiopia — to Tigray in northern Ethiopia. He grew up there with his two younger sisters. Beginning at the age of five, he worked in the fields and tended to the animals.

Petros left Ethiopia alone at the age of 16, arriving in Germany in early 2012. He was initially housed in accommodation for asylum seekers. His mother and sisters remained in Tigray.

In late 2021, due to the conflict in the region, Petros went more than two months without any contact with them.

"It's very hard," he told DW at the time. "Sometimes I sleep poorly and have bad dreams. But I try not to give up hope."

Running helped.

"If I were to give up my sport, I would have lost everything," Petros said. "I've already lost my family, and then I would have lost the last thing I have left."

The situation in Tigray weighed on his mind even during races.

"I think about my family all the time," Petros said in 2021. While running, he tries to block out those thoughts and focus on the sport.

Talent discovered on the football pitch

Shortly after he arrived in Germany, Petros started playing football, but a club official noticed his pace and hooked him up with a local athletics club. In June 2012, just months after his arrival, Petros ran his first 10-kilometer race, winning by around two and a half minutes.

Getting acclimatized to a hew country wasn't so easy.

"Learning the language was a major challenge," Petros told DW at the time. "But understanding the German mentality was an even bigger one."

He was naturalised in 2015 although at the time immigrants were usually required to wait eight years to become eligible for German citizenship. At the 2021 Olympic Games in Japan, he competed for Germany in the marathon for the first time.

In the years that followed, Petros moved closer to the international elite. In December 2025, he ran a time of 2:04:03 in Valencia, setting a new German marathon record. Another German record followed in March 2026 at the Berlin Half Marathon, where he clocked 59:22 minutes.

Near miss at Worlds

Just how close Petros had come to the world elite was evident at the World Championships in Tokyo in September 2025. He picked up the pace with 350 meters to go. He was the first to enter the stadium and, on the home straight looked like the new world champion. But Alphonce Simbu of Tanzania past him in the closing meters of the race. Both were clocked at 2:09:48. The photo finish decided the outcome: Petros missed gold by 0.03 seconds.

"As a professional athlete, I simply have to accept that and look ahead," Petros said afterwards. With silver, he secured Germany's first World Championship medal in the men's marathon since 1983.

"Achieving this is a huge deal for me, especially for my family, for my mom," he said after the race. He planned to send her videos of his run. "Hopefully, I'll be able to bring her to Germany for a competition someday."

Now, 11 months after that photo-finish loss in Tokyo, Petros has savored his first major international title in Birmingham.

"The race was incredibly, incredibly hard," Petros said. "But a bit of red wine will get me back on my feet quickly."

And just how much is "a bit"?

"Oh, you know, one, two, or three glasses."

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Fact check: How do I spot fake social media accounts, bots and trolls?
entries.summary: If you are unsure whether to trust a message on TikTok or X, study its source. The following indicators can help you determine if you are dealing with a fake account, bot or troll.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

If you are unsure whether to trust a message on TikTok or X, study its source. The following indicators can help you determine if you are dealing with a fake account, bot or troll.

Hundreds of thousands of inauthentic social media accounts. Tens of thousands of fake articles. Millions of automated posts.

These are some of the figures cited by the German Foreign Ministry in connection with a Russian disinformation campaign that was first detected in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine.

Known as Doppelgänger, the operation aimed to amplify pro-Russian narratives on social media platforms in countries like Germany.

On some days, thousands of the accounts were active, posting more than once per second in a coordinated manner, the ministry said in a 2024 report. 

This campaign underscores just how important it is for users to verify the authenticity of social media accounts and identify when content is being published or amplified by bots and trolls. 

But first, what’s the difference between a bot and a troll? And how can you spot them?

DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape. 

What are fake accounts?

Fake accounts are social media profiles that conceal their true identity. Some may pretend to be ordinary users; others can impersonate politicians, institutions or journalists.

Not all fake accounts have malicious intent. Some people may use pseudonyms to protect their identity or for security reasons. Activists or whistleblowers may use fake accounts to investigate sensitive issues.

What are bots?

Bots, short for robots, tirelessly comment on posts, share content, or artificially stoke online debate on marginal or otherwise overlooked topics. Sometimes, they’re entirely innocent, but sometimes they’re intent is harmful.

Good bots may automatically share news or weather forecasts, as well as earthquake alerts and satellite images on social media.

Bad bots, in contrast, are designed to imitate genuine human activity to advance a certain agenda. Depending on the algorithm, such computer programs may compose and publish social media posts or comments, follow others, or even send out friendship requests.

Bad bots can distort reality by amplifying certain political opinions on social media platforms and drawing artificial attention to certain issues.

What are trolls?

Trolls, on the other hand, are real human beings who exhibit destructive and hyperactive online behavior.

Some are even paid to harass certain public figures or media organizations as part of so-called troll factories or farms. 

One of the most prominent examples of a troll factory is the Internet Research Agency in St. Petersburg, Russia.

EUvsDisinfo, a project by the European External Action Service to counter disinformation, found that the agency had disseminated falsehoods and pro-Kremlin messages in multiple languages during various European and US election campaigns and in the lead-up to several referenda. 

How can you spot them?

Many of the fake accounts, bots and trolls may disappear before you even notice them.

At least in Europe, social media platforms are required under the Digital Services Act (DSA) to release transparency reports, including how much content they delete. 

In the last three months of 2025, for instance, Metareported taking action on 1.1 billion accounts.  

But sometimes accounts appear faster than platforms can take action. So here are some concrete tips than can help you identify them.

Identity: Check the account name, profile picture and handle

Genuine accounts tend to have a consistent digital identity. Their name, profile picture, bio and content generally tend to support the same story about who’s behind the account.

Be cautious if this does not appear to be the case. Potential red flags include:

  • A generic, stock-style or AI-generated profile picture
  • A username containing a long string of seemingly random characters and numbers
  • An account that was created recently and suddenly became very active
  • A generic bio, such as “Truth Seeker” or “Patriot”, with little or no personal information

Beyond this, verify the information through official channels.

Public figures typically have a traceable online presence. Look for links to official websites and organizations they work for. Check whether the account’s name, profile picture, personal information and handle are consistent with information published elsewhere.

Use the reverse image search method (for example on Google Lensor TinEye) to find out whether the picture used in the profile depicts someone else than claimed, or if the image has surfaced elsewhere online.  

And don’t rely on verification badges. While a blue check mark was once primarily used to confirm the identity of public figures and organizations, some platforms now allow users to buy them.

Behavior: Review what the account posts

Fake accounts, bots and troll accounts often behave differently from ordinary users.

Genuine users typically interact with others, discuss several topics and display natural patterns of activity that are often connected to their interests, profession or geographical location.

A German student posting images purporting to show an Afghan war zone? A Russian pensioner sharing photos from what she claims are Parisian anti-vaccination protests?

Neither is impossible, but both may warrant closer scrutiny. The accounts could be fake or they may be sharing disinformation. Suspicious behavior like this is typical of bots, too.

Bots also tend to post at a speed and frequency that would be nearly impossible for most people to sustain.

Trolls accounts, meanwhile, are harder to detect than downright fake accounts, as they are usually controlled by real human beings.

For trolls, it’s best to focus on the content they’re sharing. A troll’s defining feature is often their behavior rather than their identity.

Trolls are usually less interested in meaningful discussion than in provoking reactions. Their goal is frequently to increase engagement by generating outrage, sowing divisions or derailing conversations.

Network: Examine the account’s network and interactions

Fake accounts, bots and trolls rarely operate in isolation. You can find valuable clues about an account’s authenticity by examining who follows it and how other users interacts with it.

Genuine users tend to have a diverse mix of followers and interactions. By contrast, fake accounts are often part of networks that repeatedly amplify a particular narrative.

Here are some potential red flags:

  • Large numbers of followers with generic profile information
  • Comments or replies that are repetitive, identical or unrelated to the content of the post
  • Thousands of followers but little meaningful engagement
  • Followers that were created recently, have little posting history, or primarily repost content from other accounts
  • Conversations that appear one-sided, with little disagreement or diversity of opinions
  • Multiple accounts posting the same comments, links or hashtags within a short period

If you are unsure whether an account is fake, or whether content is being spread by a bot or a troll, slow down and take a closer look.

A few minutes spent examining an account’s identity, behavior and network can go a long way towards helping you distinguish genuine users from fake accounts, bots and trolls.

This article was first published in 2022 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. Edited by Josh Axelrod.

This article is part of a DW Fact check series on digital literacy. Other articles include:

  • How do I spot manipulated images?
  • How do I spot AI-generated images?
  • How do I spot audio deepfakes?
  • How do I spot propaganda?

And here you can read more about how DW fact-checks fake news.

entries.title: Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala collapses on pitch again
entries.summary: One of Germany's top footballers has collapsed on the pitch for a second time in four days ahead of the new season. Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala has a "neurological dysfunction" that causes blackouts.
entries.content:
Germany

Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala collapses on pitch again

August 19, 2026

One of Germany's top footballers has collapsed on the pitch for a second time in four days ahead of the new season. Bayern Munich's Jamal Musiala has a "neurological dysfunction" that causes blackouts.

Germany international Jamal Musiala has collapsed during a match for the second time in four days. He was helped off the pitch looking dazed just six minutes after coming on as a subsititute in Bayern Munich's 4-2 friendly win at Heidenheim on Tuesday. Musiala collapsed in similar fashion in a match against RB Leipzig a few days earlier.

After the Heidenheim game, Musiala explained in an Instagram post that the blackouts were caused by a "neurological dysfunction" known as "absence seizures."

"I've been diagnosed with temporary, brief, but easily treatable absence seizures, which are due to a neurological dysfunction," he wrote in the post, which drew support from many in the football world, including Bayern keeper Manuel Neuer and former Germany and Bayern forward Thomas Müller.

"These can lead to the recent episodes, like the one against Leipzig or now in Heidenheim. I know they seem scary at first glance – but for me, they're currently just part of my everyday life.

"I'm receiving excellent medical treatment and am very optimistic. FC Bayern and my family and friends are always by my side and supporting me on this journey."

What are absence seizures?

Once known as "petit mal" seizures, absence seizures are split in to two types – typical and atypical. It is not yet clear which of these Musiala is experiencing.

Typical cases cause a person to stop anything they are doing in an instant and appear to 'switch off'. Sometimes their eyes may look upwards or flutter. They last between 10 and 20 seconds and may cause some confusion for a few seconds afterwards before the person returns to their usual state.

Atypical cases usually last a little longer than typical ones and may also include chewing or lip smacking movements, hand motions or repetitive blinking.

Both are a type of epilepsy and, according to the Epilepsy Foundation, are caused by "brief abnormal electrical activity in a person's brain". They are most commonly found in children but can occur in adults and the foundation says they can be occurring for a long time before being diagnosed, depending on the environment in which they occur. It adds that some people may have "hundreds of brief absence seizures a day." Treatment is not generally required, but some medicines are available for more serious cases.

Is Jamal Musiala's career at risk?

Bayern Munich told German press agency DPA that the absence seizures were no threat to Musiala's career but it seems apparent that collapsing on the pitch will be difficult to manage if it doesn't clear up.

Although very different in nature, the seizures are another setback for a player who has struggled for fitness in recent years. Musiala, 23, broke his leg in the Club World Cup last July and found it difficult to regain fitness and form. In March he was hit by an ankle injury.

He did make the Germany World Cup squad but looked off the pace for much of the tournament. He then required a small operation to remove a metal plate from his foot left over from last year's leg operation.

What's next for Jamal Musiala and Bayern Munich?

Bayern's season begins on Saturday with the German Super Cup, rebranded as the "Franz Beckenbauer Supercup" this season. The match usually pits the German champions against the German Cup winners but, with Bayern having won both last year, they face league runners up Borussia Dortmund. They open their Bundesliga title defense the following Friday, August 28, against Stuttgart in Munich.

It is unclear whether Musiala will play any part in either of these games and how Bayern and the player will manage the seizures, but Musiala remains upbeat.

"It has been my personal desire to take on this challenge and, with the approval of the neurologists, to continue focusing on what helps me most in my recovery: simply living my everyday life and continuing to pursue my passion for playing football," Musiala wrote.

"I have taken responsibility for this. Overall, I feel very positive and am on the right track. What helps me most on this journey is continuing to chase victories and titles with my team and your amazing support."

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Nord Stream: Second suspect arrested over pipeline blasts
entries.summary: German prosecutors said a Ukrainian suspect was arrested in Croatia. They said that the man, a trained scuba diver, "is strongly suspected of jointly causing explosions."
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

German prosecutors said a Ukrainian suspect was arrested in Croatia. They said that the man, a trained scuba diver, "is strongly suspected of jointly causing explosions."

A second suspect has been arrested in relation to the Nord Stream gas pipeline explosions in 2022, German prosecutors said on Wednesday.

Croatian police, acting on a European arrest warrant, detained a Ukrainian national in Pula.

"The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office had Ukrainian Vladimir Z. arrested in Pula (Croatia) by local police forces," prosecutors said.

They said that the man, a trained scuba diver, "is strongly suspected of jointly causing explosions."

The prosecutors said they were pursuing the man's extradition from Croatia.

He is reported to have previously been detained in Poland in September 2025 but was released after an extradition request from Germany was turned down.

Another suspect, also a Ukrainian national, was arrested in Italy last year.

What happened to the Nord Stream pipelines?

The Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines were set up to deliver Russian gas to Germany and other countries in Europe.

Nord Stream 2 had yet to enter service when in September 2022, both pipelines were damaged by blasts that rendered them inoperable.

The blasts came just months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Germany has said it believes the blasts were sabotage ordered by unspecified Ukrainian state entities but Kyiv has so far denied involvement.

Prosecutors have said the plot aimed to permanently disrupt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Moscow from using the revenue generated from natural gas trading to finance its military operations.

Moscow had repeatedly reduced or suspended deliveries through Nord Stream 1 after starting the invasion, blaming Western sanctions and technical issues.

Europe, in its turn, accused Russia of weaponizing energy supplies.

More to follow...

entries.title: Nick Kyrgios suspended after testing positive for cocaine
entries.summary: Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for cocaine. The 31-year-old apologized to his fans, saying he'd "made a huge mistake."
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for cocaine. The 31-year-old apologized to his fans, saying he'd "made a huge mistake."

Former Wimbledon finalist Nick Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended from tennis after failing a doping test, the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) announced on Wednesday.

The 31-year-old Australian gave a sample at an ATP tournament in Mallorca in June that tested positive for benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, the ITIA said.

Cocaine is classified as a stimulant and substance of abuse on the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Prohibited List and is banned in competition.

A WADA lab confirmed the presence of the banned stimulant in Kyrgios' sample on July 17, and a provisional suspension has been in place since August 4, the ITIA said.

"While suspended Kyrgios is not allowed to play in, coach at, or attend any events organiZed or sanctioned by World Tennis, WTA, ATP, the Grand Slams, or any national association," the agency added.

Kyrgios apologizes to fans

Kyrgios apologized to his fans in a statement on social media, saying he took "full responsibility."

"I made ​a huge mistake," he said. "I'm sorry to my fans, my family, my sponsors and everyone close to me. Above all, I'm sorry to the kids who follow me. I know the example this sets and I'm deeply disappointed in myself."

Known for his big serve, Kyrgios has won seven singles titles on the ATP tour and reached a high of 13 in the world in 2016.

His best performance was perhaps at the Wimbledon final in 2022, where he lost in four sets to Novak Djokovic.

Physical and mental toll of injuries

Since then, he has been plagued by multiple injuries and hasn't been able to return to form. He is currently ranked number 919 in the world.

In his statement on Wednesday, Kyrgios said that his injuries took "a huge toll on me both physically and mentally."

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do, and coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined," he said.

The Australian has not appealed the provisional suspension and said he would step away from social media and public life for 28 days to "focus on getting myself right."

"I'm sorry, I'll do the work and come back better," he said.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Germany news: Minister wants to help renters to install AC
entries.summary: The justice minister wants to make it easier for tenants to install air conditioning or external blinds. Meanwhile, a defense CEO is reportedly in hiding after being warned of Russian plots to kill him. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Minister wants to help renters to install AC

Published August 19, 2026last updated August 19, 2026

The justice minister wants to make it easier for tenants to install air conditioning or external blinds. Meanwhile, a defense CEO is reportedly in hiding after being warned of Russian plots to kill him. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says laws on rented accommodation could be changed to allow tenants to improve their protection against heat
  • Hubig also spoke out in favor of enshrining climate adaptation measures in the constitution as proposed by her Social Democratic Party
  • Reports say the CEO of an arms startup supplying attack drones to Ukraine has been in hiding for months after being warned of a Russian assassination plot

This is a roundup of the top headlines from and about Germany on August 19, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Merz condemns 'unacceptable' remarks by Israeli security minister — spokesman

Merz condemns 'unacceptable' remarks by Israeli security minister — spokesman

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has described as "inhumane" remarks ⁠made ⁠by far-right Israeli Security Minister ​Itamar Ben-Gvir advocating the targeted killing of Palestinians in Gaza, a government spokesman ​said on ‌Wednesday.

"The chancellor strongly condemns the inhumane appeals made by Minister Ben-Gvir, which violate international law," spokesman Sebastian Hille said. "They are unacceptable."

 Ben-Gvir made the remarks during a podcast with Rom Braslavski, a former hostage held in Gaza after the October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel by Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups.

"I think that targeted killings should be carried out in Gaza, removing 30, 40 people every night," he said in the podcast, which was broadcast on Saturday.

Ben-Gvir added that he meant not only militant Palestinians who were an immediate threat but other people in the Gaza Strip who he said did not deserve to live.

On Tuesday, Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil also sharply criticized what he called the "dehumanizing" remarks by Ben-Gvir and said sanctions on him at the European level should now be considered "very seriously."

Skip next section Ever more foreign qualifications recognized in Germany — Destatis

Ever more foreign qualifications recognized in Germany — Destatis

Germany is accepting the qualifications of a growing number of foreign professionals, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) reported on Wednesday.

It said authorities had approved 86,600 applications last year, almost 10% more than in 2024.

That rise is, however, smaller than in 2024 and 2023, which saw the number of approvals increase by 21% and 25% respectively.

As in previous years, most of those accepted in 2025 came from Turkey (9,800), accounting for 11% of overall approvals. Around 8,300 recognitions from Ukraine were also reported.

Most of the recognized qualifications were in medical professions, as was also the case in 2024.

Nursing professionals had 32,000 applications approved, followed by doctors (13,900).

There were also 4,600 acceptances for engineers, meaning that those three professions together made up more than half (58%) of recognitions.

A number of sectors in Germany are relying ever more on foreign professionals as the birth rate falls and the population ages.

Skip next section Investigation bureau gives details on near-accident in Munich

Investigation bureau gives details on near-accident in Munich

Germany's Federal Bureau of Aircraft Accident Investigation (BFU) has said the causes of a near-accident at the weekend involving a Vietnam Airlines aircraft were still unclear but presented details on the incident.

In a statement issued late on Tuesday, the BFU said the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner started its takeoff at Munich Airport at 1:57 pm (1157 GMT) on Saturday and was late getting into the air.

It said the tail touched the ground just before lift-off and that tire marks had been found at the end of the runway that were probably from the aircraft.

The plane eventually turned around, landing back at Munich Airport at 3:58 p.m.

The agency said its experts were currently analyzing the plane's flight recorders and that authorities in Vietnam and the US were also participating in the investigation.

"The investigation does not serve to establish blame, liability or claims," the authority said, but rather was intended to help prevent any such accidents and incidents in future.

Experts have said that the 270 passengers and crew on board the plane narrowly escaped disaster.

The aircraft had great difficulty taking off despite the pilot's efforts to pull the nose up.

When it landed two hours later, smoke was visible from the undercarriage and tires had burst. Passengers and crew were uninjured.

Skip next section Tenants should be able to install heat protection more easily — justice minister

Tenants should be able to install heat protection more easily — justice minister

Laws on rented accommodation could potentially be changed to allow tenants more freedom in adapting their apartments to cope with heat ways, Federal Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig has said.

"Conventional legal policy can also make a contribution to heat protection," she told the daily Rheinische Post in an interview published on Wednesday morning.

"I am thinking about tenancy laws in particular," she said. "I can imagine, for example, that we make it easier for tenants to equip their apartments with air conditioning or sun shades."

At present, tenants have no legal right to install built-in air conditioning devices or external shades but need permission from their rental owner.

Hubig also spoke out in favor of the proposal made by her Social Democratic Party to enshrine climate protection in the German constitution, or Basic Law, as a joint obligation of both the federal government and state administrations. Currently, the primary responsibility for heat protections lies with the states and municipalities.

"This would make it easier for the government to give states and municipalities sustained support in heat-protection measures," she said.

Germany, like much of ‌Europe, has experienced ⁠successive ⁠heat waves this summer with temperatures repeatedly approaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit). This has reignited public debate over the use of air conditioners, which remain rare in the country.

Skip next section Runaway sheep goes through bus wash

Runaway sheep goes through bus wash

A German sheep has probably had the experience of its life after it boarded an empty bus that was then driven through a bus wash.

The sheep had escaped from its home in the western town of Lüdinghausen and gone aboard the bus at the local bus depot, police said on Tuesday.

According to the transport company RVM, the sheep entered the bus as it was about to be cleaned in the depot's wash hall, causing officers to be called to the scene.

The police then escorted the vehicle as it went through the wash to prevent the sheep escaping, as the bus was already in such a position that it could not back out of the facility.

The owner then collected the animal after what must have been a confusing ride for it.

RVM said the sheep was one of several that had run across the depot grounds during the incident a few days ago.

Skip next section Defense startup CEO living under ground due to Russian plots — reports

Defense startup CEO living under ground due to Russian plots — reports

The head of a German defense startup that is supplying attack drones to Ukraine as it defends itself against invading Russian troops has been in hiding for months after warnings that he was at risk of his life from Russian agents, reports said on Tuesday.

Donaustahl CEO Stefan Thumann told private broadcaster RTL and magazine Stern in a joint interview that he had received warnings from German officials in late 2025 that Russian intelligence was plotting against his life.

"I'm fighting a duel with the Russian military intelligence service for my life," he said.

"Constantly changing locations, 24-hour personal security, my private life has ceased to exist," he added.

Thumann said he now slept next to his computer and started working as soon as he woke up to distract himself from his personal situation.

In March, prosecutors said they had arrested two so-called disposable agents who were alleged to have spied on Thumann to prepare an assassination attempt.

Disposable agents is the name given to people with little training who are hired by military intelligence services for small pay to carry out missions.

But RTL cited a German lawmaker who said there were still plans targeting him that were well advanced and involved using a nerve agent.

In 2024, the United States thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of German defense giant Rheinmetall, Armin Papperger, according to a CNN report. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW's newsroom in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag!

Today, we will be looking at proposals by the Social Democrat justice minister to change the law to make it easier for tenants to install heat protective measures as heat waves increase in frequency and severity.

And as Russia continues with its strategy of hybrid warfare against the West, reports say that the CEO of a German defense startup is living in constant fear of his life amid warnings of a Russian plot against him.

On a lighter note, we also have the story of a runaway sheep that boarded an empty bus and got to experience the thrill of the vehicle going through the wash facility.

Read on for details on these stories and more.

entries.title: Who really owns the Caspian Sea?
entries.summary: Five countries border the Caspian Sea, but none owns a fixed share. A 2018 convention established rules for navigation, security and fishing while leaving some seabed borders unresolved.
entries.content:
August 19, 2026

Five countries border the Caspian Sea, but none owns a fixed share. A 2018 convention established rules for navigation, security and fishing while leaving some seabed borders unresolved.

For decades, debate in Iran over the Caspian Sea has often centered on a deceptively simple question: What percentage belongs to the country?

Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan all border the body of water. But the Caspian is treated neither as a conventional sea nor simply as an international lake.

Instead, the five countries have developed a special legal regime governing navigation, territorial waters, fishing, security and seabed resources.

The most important step came in 2018, when the five presidents signed the Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea in Aktau, Kazakhstan.

It established territorial waters of up to 15 nautical miles and an additional 10-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone for each country. But it did not divide the entire Caspian into five fixed national shares.

Why doesn't Iran own half the Caspian Sea

Before the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Iran and the Soviet Union were the only two countries bordering the Caspian.

The 1921 Russo-Persian Treaty of Friendship restored Iranian navigation rights restricted under Imperial Russia. A 1940 treaty further regulated trade and navigation.

None of the agreements, however, awarded Iran 50% of the Caspian.

Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, says that this distinction is central to understanding the dispute.

"None of these treaties specified a percentage for either Iran or the Soviet Union," he told DW. "They emphasized common use rather than dividing the sea into ownership shares."

After the Soviet collapse, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan emerged as independent states, turning a bilateral legal arrangement into a five-country negotiation.

Some Iranian politicians argued for a 50% share since it had previously shared the sea with the Soviet Union alone; others called for 20%. So far, neither claim has gained international recognition.

What the 2018 Caspian Sea agreement settled

"The Caspian is neither completely a sea nor completely a lake," Vakhshiteh said.

"The 2018 convention created a special legal regime that distinguishes between the water, seabed, security and resources," he added.

The convention does not divide the surface into national sectors. Each country has territorial waters and fishing zones, while other areas remain available for common navigation.

The seabed can be divided through agreements between neighboring states. These agreements matter because offshore oil and gas rights depend largely on such boundaries.

Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have already reached several bilateral delimitation agreements. Iran's southern boundaries remain among the more politically sensitive issues.

How security became central to Caspian Sea politics

The 2018 convention prohibits the presence of armed forces belonging to non-bordering states in the Caspian. Coastal countries are also not supposed to allow their territory to be used for military action against a neighboring Caspian state.

But Iran recently accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian, killing a sailor. Kyiv said it had targeted vessels involved in transporting military cargo linked to Iran and Russia.

Vakhshiteh argues that such incidents demonstrate why Tehran considers keeping outside military powers away from the Caspian a strategic priority.

"Iran may still negotiate over seabed boundaries, but on one important principle a common legal rule already exists: the Caspian should not become a military base for powers from outside the region," he said.

Currently, Iran is the only one of the five signatories that has not completed parliamentary ratification of the convention.

Oil and gas in the Caspian Sea

Behind the legal and military debates is another major issue: energy in the form of oil and gas.

Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan have developed substantial offshore oil resources, while Turkmenistan possesses major natural gas reserves.

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, says that Iran has meaningful hydrocarbon potential, too.

Its most important Caspian discovery, Sardar-e Jangal, was found in 2012 but development has been slow and it has not entered commercial production.

Iranian estimates suggest the area may contain around 2 billion barrels of oil, with roughly 500 million potentially recoverable, plus natural gas.

"Iran has confirmed hydrocarbon discoveries and promising prospects, but its commercially recoverable Caspian resource base remains uncertain and largely undeveloped," Shokri told DW.

The southern Caspian is significantly deeper than many of the areas developed by Iran's neighbors. Sardar-e Jangal lies in water around 700 meters deep, requiring advanced drilling equipment, subsea technology and substantial investment.

Sanctions have made access to international companies, financing and specialized offshore technology much harder. The country also has simpler options.

"Iran has huge oil and gas fields in the Persian Gulf and onshore that are generally easier and cheaper to develop," Shokri said.

For Tehran, investing billions in difficult deepwater Caspian projects has often been less attractive than expanding production around the Persian Gulf like its South Pars gas field.

So, who owns the Caspian?

In the end, no single country owns or controls the Caspian Sea. And no treaty gives Iran, Russia or any other state a fixed share of the body of water.

The five neighboring states have territorial waters and exclusive fishing zones, while other parts remain open to common use.

Seabed boundaries, which determine many offshore oil and gas rights, are negotiated separately between neighboring countries. For Iran, that means some of its offshore resource rights are still subject to negotiation.

But ownership percentage is no longer the central question.

Today, the bigger issues are a combination of how the Caspian's resources are managed, where maritime boundaries are drawn and its ability to keep out external military forces.

Edited by: Tim Rooks
